Learning Objectives
Review the anatomy and biomechanics of the sesamoids and explain their role in hallux
metatarsophalangeal joint function.
Explain the appropriate workup for a patient with sesamoid pain, including a clinical
examination and appropriate imaging studies.
Distinguish features of a sesamoid fracture from those of other sesamoid pathology.
Identify clinical features and explain the workup for a sesamoid stress fracture, including a
physical examination and appropriate imaging studies.
Outline nonsurgical and surgical treatment options for sesamoid stress fractures.
Review the anatomy and biomechanics of the hallux metatarsophalangeal joint relevant to turf
toe injuries.
Explain the appropriate workup for turf toe injuries, including a clinical examination and
appropriate imaging studies.

List surgical indications for and explain the surgical management of turf toe injuries.
Sesamoid Fractures
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The tibial (medial) sesamoid and fibular (lateral) sesamoid are embedded in the flexor hallucis
brevis (FHB) at the level of the first metatarsal head.
The tibial sesamoid is larger than the fibular sesamoid and more vulnerable to injury.1
Held together by the intersesamoid ligament
Typically ossify by age 8 years in girls and age 12 years in boys2
Incomplete fusion results in bipartite or multipartite sesamoid.
33.5% incidence, 25% likelihood of bilaterality3
Bipartite fibular sesamoid is rare.
The tibial sesamoid attaches to the abductor hallucis.
The fibular sesamoid attaches to the oblique/transverse heads of the adductor hallucis.
Both sesamoids attach to the metatarsal head via the medial and lateral sesamoid ligament.
The sesamoid complex absorbs more than 300% of body weight during push-off.4
Blood supply limited4
Primarily extraosseous
Plantar blood supply: proper plantar artery and first plantar metatarsal artery
Distal blood supply: synovial capsule, low volume
Function to provide mechanical advantage by increasing the lever arm of the FHB, protecting
the flexor hallucis longus (FHL) and dissipating forces to the hallux metatarsophalangeal (MTP)
joint
Mechanism of Injury
Direct trauma: Typical mechanism of injury is forced dorsiflexion of the hallux or a crush injury.
Severe dorsiflexion may result in complete disruption of the plantar soft tissues (turf toe).
Associated with sports that involve repetitive dorsiflexion of the hallux and considerable
impact to the area of the sesamoids
More commonly involves the tibial sesamoid
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:10 PM
AAOS | Forefoot Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004101
2/22

77% of sesamoid fractures are tibial, 23% of sesamoid fractures are fibular.5
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Acute fractures typically present as sudden pain from an inciting injury.
Pain with weight bearing, altered gait to avoid push-off under hallux
Passive range of motion (ROM) of the hallux MTP joint often is painful.
Direct palpation of the sesamoid localizes pain to the fractured sesamoid.
Resisted plantar flexion of the hallux MTP joint exacerbates pain.
Imaging studies
Bilateral weight-bearing AP, lateral, 40° medial/lateral oblique foot radiographs (axial
sesamoid view if possible; Figure 1)
Figure 1 Axial sesamoid radiograph demonstrates a fracture of the tibial sesamoid. (Courtesy
of John Campbell, MD , Baltimore, MD.)
Acute fracture versus bipartite/multipartite
Bilaterally, a symmetric location of partition and a smooth, well-corticated outline are
features indicative of bipartite/multipartite sesamoid.6
Bipartite/multipartite sesamoids typically are larger in size than unipartite sesamoids.7
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:10 PM
AAOS | Forefoot Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004101
3/22

Acute fracture is associated with an irregular pattern, sharp edges, and comminution.
Other findings: hallux MTP joint alignment, sesamoid retraction/diastasis
MRI can distinguish soft-tissue pathology from osseous abnormalities.
Fractures: low signal intensity fracture line observed on T1-weighted images (sagittal view),
extensive edema observed on T2-weighted images (Figure 2)
CT useful to interpret acute fractures and arthritis
Bridging callus formation may indicate healing.
Figure 2 Coronal (A) and sagittal (B) T2-weighted MRIs of a tibial sesamoid show a low signal
intensity fracture line and extensive edema. (Courtesy of Rebecca A. Cerrato, MD, Baltimore, MD.)

Evaluation and Diagnosis
Treating providers should consider the possibility of a sesamoid fracture in evaluating
patients, particularly athletes, who have pain about the hallux. A diagnosis of a sesamoid
fracture is first made via a physical examination. Patients frequently present with
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:10 PM
AAOS | Forefoot Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004101
4/22

activity-related plantar hallux pain. The high prevalence of bipartite/multipartite
sesamoids makes distinguishing them from fractures difficult.
Management and Outcomes
Non–weight-bearing cast for 6 weeks8
Walker boot for 4 to 6 more weeks
Surgical management
Indications: wide displacement, associated unstable turf toe, painful nonunion
Percutaneous screw fixation9
Bone grafting and internal fixation
Partial excision
Biedert and Hintermann1 reported on five athletes who underwent proximal pole excision.
All the athletes returned to sport within 6 months.
Complete sesamoidectomy: most common surgical procedure used for failed nonsurgical
management10, 12
Medial approach (slightly plantar to the standard medial approach): tibial sesamoid
Protect the medial plantar cutaneous nerve.
Longitudinal capsulotomy
Sesamoid excision performed extra-articular, protecting the FHL
Repair the FHB complex; advance the abductor hallucis if the defect substantial.
Plantarlateral or dorsolateral approach: fibular sesamoid
The plantarlateral approach is preferred for access and protection of the plantar
hallucal nerve along the plantar hallucal crease.
The FHB tendon complex is repaired.
Complications
Increased load to residual sesamoid
Tibial sesamoid resection: hallux valgus
Fibular sesamoid resection: hallux varus

Management and Outcomes
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:10 PM
AAOS | Forefoot Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004101
5/22

The management of sesamoid fractures is most commonly accomplished nonsurgically,
with more than 90% of patients becoming pain-free without surgical treatment.13
Recovery may take more than 6 months, highlighting that recovery from these injuries
may be prolonged. Sesamoid factures are difficult to manage because of their poor
blood supply and the forces they encounter during weight bearing. Surgical treatment
options include bone grafting nonunion, partial excision, and complete sesamoidectomy.
Sesamoid Stress Fractures
Mechanism of Injury
Chronic, repetitive stress
Ballet dancing, running, and barefoot sports are associated with a higher incidence of
sesamoid stress fractures.14
Represent 4% of foot and ankle injuries in runners15
Comprise 1% to 3% of all stress fractures16

Mechanism of Injury
Stress fractures of the hallux MTP joint sesamoids commonly are associated with sports
that involve forced repetitive dorsiflexion of the great toe. These injuries comprise 1% to
3% of all stress fractures.16 The tibial sesamoid is larger, subject to greater weight-
bearing forces, and more commonly injured.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Pain with weight bearing and altered gait to avoid push-off under hallux (similar to acute stress
fracture) but no history of an acute injury
On clinical examination, patients often lack ecchymosis or swelling.
Tenderness to palpation over the involved sesamoid and pain with passive dorsiflexion and
resisted plantar flexion are common.
Imaging studies
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:10 PM
AAOS | Forefoot Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004101
6/22

Radiography
Often normal
MRI often required to confirm diagnosis
Marrow edema replaces normal marrow signal; only slightly decreased signal intensity
observed on T1-weighted images.6
Sesamoiditis and osteonecrosis may have a similar appearance.
CT—sagittal and coronal CT scans are the most reliable imaging study to detect a stress
fracture1

Evaluation and Diagnosis
The diagnosis of a sesamoid stress fracture is clinical. A stress fracture should be
considered in patients with activity-related pain and swelling under the hallux MTP joint.
Dissimilar from acute fractures, radiographs may appear normal.17
Management and Outcomes
Considered high-risk stress fracture of the foot/ankle because they often require more
aggressive management, such as restricted–weight bearing or surgical managemnet18
Initial management is nonsurgical.
Restricted–weight bearing, activity cessation; persistent pain may necessitate a course of
non–weight bearing.
NSAIDs, shoe wear modifications (stiffer sole to limit hallux MTP joint dorsiflexion, rocker
sole)
Orthotics: sesamoid relief, steel shank19
Surgical management considered for pain lasting more than 6 months
Bone grafting if less than 2 mm diastasis, no cystic change/osteonecrosis/arthritic changes20,
21
Internal fixation or sesamoidectomy for displacement
Sesamoidectomy most common reported technique22
Sesamoidectomy allows for more rapid return to sports activity; internal fixation affords the
best possible return to pre-injury function.23
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:10 PM
AAOS | Forefoot Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004101
7/22


Management and Outcomes
Sesamoid stress fractures initially are managed nonsurgically via a period of activity
cessation or modification for 2 to 6 months.5 In a systematic review of all studies
reporting return-to-sport rates and time after the management of hallux sesamoid
stress fractures, Robertson et al22 reported that no randomized clinical trials were
available. Nonsurgical management offered limited success in return to pre-injury level,
limited at 64%. Clinicians should recognize a poor response; if documented, surgical
management should be considered. Sesamoidectomy offered the quickest return to
sports activity. Patients with a fibular sesamoid stress fracture return to sport sooner
than those with a tibial sesamoid stress fracture.
Turf Toe Injuries
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Static stabilizers: capsule, collateral ligaments, plantar plate
Dynamic stabilizers: FHB, sesamoids and adductor and abductor hallucis tendons
Medial (tibial) and lateral (fibular) sesamoids lie within the FHB and are positioned directly
under the hallux metatarsal head. They support the first MTP joint by reducing the force
applied to the joint and protect the FHL.
The plantar plate, a dense fibrous band, connects the sesamoids to the plantar base of the
first proximal phalanx.
The abductor and adductor hallucis tendons insert on the medial and lateral bases of the
proximal phalanx, also giving off small attachments to the sesamoids. The medial and lateral
collateral ligaments, connecting the proximal phalanx and the first metatarsal head, provide
varus and valgus stability.
Hallux MTP joint ROM: active restricted to 55° of dorsiflexion and 25° of plantar flexion;
passive dorsiflexion can be tolerated to 75°.23

Anatomy and Biomechanics
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:10 PM
AAOS | Forefoot Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004101
8/22

The hallux MTP joint is considered a hinge joint with a sliding component. The shallow
groove of the proximal phalanx base creates an inherent degree of instability. The joint
relies on static and dynamic stabilizers. In a biomechanical study, Frimenko et al24
developed an injury risk curve that predicted a 50% risk of a turf toe injury if dorsiflexion
exceeds 78°.
Epidemiology
First described in 1976 by Bowers and Martin,25 who reported an increased incidence of first
MTP joint toe sprains with the widespread installation of artificial turf fields, giving these
injuries the name turf toe injuries
Turf toe injuries are one of most common foot injuries that occur in American football,
comprising 0.83% of all injuries sustained by football players in the National Collegiate Athletic
Association (NCAA).26
National Football League: 72% of players had a history of foot or ankle injuries, 10.9% of which
were turf toe injuries or MTP joint dislocations.27
Newer turf technology and better shoe wear are associated with a reduced incidence.23
Also observed in athletes participating in basketball, soccer, gymnastics, and dancing28

Epidemiology
Turf toe injuries inherited the name from the artificial turf fields used in the 1970s in
professional football. Harder than natural grass, artificial fill fields led to an 85%
increased risk of turf toe injury.26 Newer generation artificial no-fill turf fields and stiffer
athletic cleats have reduced the risk of turf toe injury.
Mechanism of Injury
The typical mechanism of a turf toe injury is an axial load on the first MTP joint with a fixed
equinus foot. The load drives the hallux into hyperextension, resulting in attenuation or
disruption of the plantar joint complex.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:10 PM
AAOS | Forefoot Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004101
9/22

Alternatively, the injury may occur if an individual falls back onto their own heel with the toe
hyperextended and the foot plantarflexed.8
Hallux position and the direction of the injury force may result in variations in the injury
pattern.
Traumatic hallux valgus deformity—Valgus directed force results in greater injury to the
medial and plantarmedial ligamentous structures.29
Artificial turf and flexible athletic cleats are associated with an increased incidence of
hyperextension injuries.26, 30
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Mild sprain: localized tenderness to the plantar first MTP joint
Severe sprain: considerable swelling, ecchymosis, diffuse tenderness, patient unwilling to push
off the hallux during ambulation
Physical examination
Palpation of the plantar capsule, collateral ligaments, sesamoids
Tenderness proximal to the sesamoids suggests an FHB strain, a low-grade injury.31
Restricted ROM
Varus/valgus stress to assess the collaterals, vertical or dorsoplantar drawer test to assess
plantar plate integrity (Figure 3)
Compare with the contralateral hallux
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:10 PM
AAOS | Forefoot Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004101
10/22

Figure 3 Clinical photograph shows the vertical or dorsoplantar drawer test to assess stability
of the plantar structures. The proximal phalanx is stressed in a dorsal direction as the
examiner’s hand stabilizes the first metatarsal. (Courtesy of Rebecca A. Cerrato, MD, Baltimore,
MD.)
Imaging studies
Bilateral weight-bearing AP, lateral, 40° medial/lateral oblique foot radiographs (axial
sesamoid view if possible)
Sesamoid location
Distal sesamoid to joint distance: less than or equal to 3 mm (tibial), less than or equal to
2.7 mm (fibular)32 (Figure 4)
Lateral dorsiflexion stress view: 3 mm or more of proximal migration is highly predictive of
severe injury, necessitating surgical management.33
Avulsion fractures, joint dislocation
Sesamoid fractures or diastasis
Forced dorsiflexion lateral radiograph
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:10 PM
AAOS | Forefoot Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004101
11/22

The sesamoids should migrate distally with passive hyperextension of the hallux MTP
joint.23
Live fluoroscopy can be used to evaluate dynamic tracking of the sesamoids with hallux
ROM.
MRI complements the physical examination but is not necessary for the diagnosis of an acute
turf toe injury.
Useful to visualize and grade injuries based on the integrity of the plantar structures
A normal plantar plate displays a homogenously low signal intensity on all pulse sequences.
Partial-thickness tear: increased intrasubstance signal intensity, thickening/thinning of the
plantar plate34
Full-thickness tear: discontinuity, retraction, fluid gap (Figure 5)
Can identify bone marrow edema, effusion, dorsal metatarsal articular impaction
Sagittal and coronal images best highlight the plantar surface and the sesamoids.35
MRI may overestimate the severity of injury in the acute setting.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:10 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004101
12/22

Figure 4 AP weight-bearing bilateral foot radiograph demonstrates proximal migration of the
medial and lateral sesamoids at the right hallux metatarsophalangeal joint. (Courtesy of John
Campbell, MD, Baltimore, MD.)
SEND FEEDBACK

13/22

Figure 5 Sagittal MRIs of a foot with a full-thickness tear. A, T2-weighted MRI shows a full-
thickness tear of the plantar plate, with discontinuity and a fluid gap. B, T1-weighted MRI shows
proximal migration of the tibial sesamoid. (Courtesy of Rebecca A. Cerrato, MD, Baltimore, MD.)

Evaluation and Diagnosis
Turf toe injuries may be subtle and require a high index of suspicion by physicians and
trainers. Careful examination of the hallux involves inspection for ecchymosis and
swelling, systematic palpation of relevant structures, and careful ROM maneuvers to
assess stability. Radiographic evaluation is mandatory in patients in whom a turf toe
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:10 PM
AAOS | Forefoot Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004101
14/22

injury is suspected. MRI can provide information on the extent of plantar plate
disruption and aid in grading the severity of injury.
Classification
First classification system devised by Clanton and Ford,36with recent revisions
Anderson37 classification: combines clinical, radiographic, and MRI findings (Table 1)

Management and Outcomes
Grade I
Does not require non–weight bearing
Use of a carbon-fiber insert or a stiff shoe for 6 to 8 weeks to limit dorsiflexion at the hallux
MTP joint
Low-impact activities are initiated, and the patient can return to sports activity as tolerated.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:10 PM
AAOS | Forefoot Trauma
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004101
15/22

Athletes typically do not miss a substantial amount of time from sports activity.31
Grade II
Often requires a period of non–weight bearing in a walking boot
Gentle ROM of the hallux is carefully initiated to prevent joint stiffness after acute pain and
swelling resolve.
Gradual weight-bearing and low-impact exercise are initiated after the patient is pain-free.
Return to sports activity includes taping the hallux to minimize dorsiflexion and orthotics.
Athletes often are out of their sport for at least 2 weeks.31
Grade III
Requires a longer period of immobilization and non–weight bearing (often 8 weeks or more);
often, more than 6 months are required for recovery.
Prolonged immobilization will result in stiffness at the hallux MTP joint, necessitating
extensive physical therapy.
Painless passive dorsiflexion is required to return to running or jumping.31
Surgical management
Indications for the surgical management of grade III injuries: unstable hallux MTP joint,
diastasis of bipartite sesamoid, sesamoid fracture, sesamoid retraction, traumatic hallux
valgus, vertical instability, loose body in joint, chondral injury, failed nonsurgical
management37, 38
Surgical technique: repair/reconstruction of the plantar capsular ligamentous complex
Medial J incision (Figure 6); two-incision technique considered for complete capsular
ligament rupture.
Identify and protect the plantarmedial digital nerve (Figure 7).
End-to-end suture repair of the plantar soft tissues or suture anchors at the plantar base of
the proximal phalanx with the toe plantarflexed 5°39, 40
Sesamoid fracture: open reduction and internal fixation, partial excision, and rare
sesamoidectomy

and protected during surgical management of turf toe. (Courtesy of John Campbell, MD,

Baltimore, MD.)
Postoperative protocol41
Hallux splinted in plantar flexion in a toe spica splint
Non–weight bearing for 4 weeks
Gentle passive ROM is initiated at week 1 postoperatively, avoiding excessive dorsiflexion.
Protected–weight bearing initiated in a boot at 4 week postoperatively; transition to a stiff-
sole shoe and turf toe plate at 8 week postopertively.
Impact activities introduced at approximately 12 weeks postoperatively
Reported outcomes
Coker et al42: eight turf toe injuries in collegiate athletics; unclear how many of the injuries
required surgical management; long-term pain and stiffness were reported.
Clanton et al43: 56 turf toe injuries (1 required surgical management); 96% occurred on
artificial turf; 95% of players returned to sports activity; 50% had persistent pain and
stiffness.
Anderson37: 19 high-level athletes with a turf toe injury; 9 required surgical treatment; 17
returned to full athletic activity.
George et al26: 147 turf toe injuries in NCAA football players; less than 2% required surgical
management; 14 times more likely to sustain injury in a game than in practice.

Management and Outcomes
Most turf toe injuries are managed nonsurgically. In analysis of data from an NCAA injury
surveillance system, George et al26 found that only 1.74% of NCAA football players with a
turf toe injury required surgical treatment. Management focuses on reducing
inflammation and pain via rest, ice, elevation, and protected–weight bearing in a boot or
toe spica cast in the acute phase. After pain and swelling are reduced, physical therapy is
initiated. Return to play begins after pain is absent.
Although most turf toe injuries can be successfully managed nonsurgically, surgical
management is necessary for some injuries to restore stability of the joint. Surgical
repair of the ruptured phalangeal sesamoid ligament complex includes repair or excision
of the fractured sesamoid. Currently, no prospective randomized controlled trials have

18/22

compared treatment options for turf toe injuries, and no evidence-based treatment
guidelines currently are available.44
